title: Valparaiso Upsets Purdue with Buzzer‑Beating 3‑Pointer in Double Overtime, Ends 0‑2 Streak Since 1976
body:
A dramatic buzzer‑beating three‑pointer in the second overtime gave Valparaiso a 83‑80 upset over Purdue on Friday night, snapping the Boilermakers’ hopes of an early‑season surge and marking their first 0‑2 start since 1976. Entering the contest as 19.5‑point favorites, Purdue seemed poised to dominate a non‑conference opponent, but the Crusaders rallied from a 12‑point deficit in the second half and forced two extra periods before clinching the victory on a last‑second shot by senior guard Ryan Haggerty.

The game’s turning point arrived early in the second half when Purdue, led by senior forward Zach Edey’s 22 points and 12 rebounds, built a 68‑56 lead with just under six minutes left. Valparaiso responded with a flurry of three‑pointers from junior guard Jaden Ricks, cutting the margin to three points at the end of regulation. Both teams exchanged baskets in the first overtime, finishing the period tied at 73. In the second overtime, the Crusaders’ relentless defense forced Purdue into a series of missed free throws, while Valparaiso’s bench contributed crucial points, including a clutch three from sophomore forward Malik Jones. When the clock expired, Haggerty’s deep shot found nothing but net, sending the home crowd into stunned silence.

The upset reverberates beyond a single loss. Purdue, a perennial contender in the Big Ten and a regular fixture in the NCAA tournament, had been expected to use the early non‑conference schedule to solidify its identity under third‑year head coach Matt Painter. Instead, the defeat exposed vulnerabilities in Purdue’s perimeter defense and its reliance on interior scoring. Edey’s dominance in the paint was offset by the Crusaders’ ability to stretch the floor, forcing the Boilermakers to guard three‑point range—a weakness that opponents will likely probe in upcoming conference play. Moreover, Purdue’s free‑throw shooting, a 65 percent effort in the two overtime periods, proved costly in a game ultimately decided by a single point.

For Valparaiso, the victory represents a watershed moment for a program that has struggled to find consistency since its 1998 run to the Sweet Sixteen. Coach Matt Lottich, in his seventh season, praised his team’s resilience: “We never stopped believing, even when we were down double digits. The guys trusted each other and executed when it mattered.” The Crusaders’ balanced attack—four players in double figures and a bench that contributed 18 points—suggests a depth that could make them a dark horse in the Missouri Valley Conference. Their ability to thrive under pressure, as demonstrated by Haggerty’s composure with the ball in his hands for the final shot, may serve as a blueprint for the rest of the season.

Purdue’s response will be closely watched. The Boilermakers head to their next game against a mid‑major opponent with a clear need to address both mental toughness and strategic adjustments. Painter is expected to emphasize ball movement and tighter perimeter coverage in practice, while also reinforcing the importance of finishing free throws. The loss could serve as a catalyst for growth, prompting the team to tighten up its fundamentals before the grueling conference schedule begins in earnest.

Looking ahead, the ripple effects of this upset could reshape the early narrative of the 2026‑27 college basketball season. Valparaiso’s triumph injects excitement into the mid‑major landscape, while Purdue must regroup quickly to avoid a domino effect that could jeopardize its tournament aspirations. As the season unfolds, both programs will be measured by how they adapt: whether the Crusaders can build on this signature win and whether the Boilermakers can translate the lessons of a painful defeat into renewed vigor on the hardwood.
